name: Butterfly Guard to Williams Guard
description: Enter Williams Guard from Butterfly Guard in no-gi BJJ. Trap the opponent's arm with a deep overhook and figure-four shoulder lock to open sweeps and submissions.
summary: Butterfly Guard to Williams Guard is a no-gi entry where the seated bottom player secures a deep overhook on the opponent's arm and threads a figure-four shoulder lock, converting butterfly hook control into the joint-threatening Williams Guard.
overview:
Butterfly Guard to Williams Guard is the primary entry into the modern shoulder-lock guard popularized by Roy Williams, executed from a seated butterfly base in no-gi. The bottom player begins with butterfly hooks and a same-side overhook on the opponent's arm, then collapses the elbow and threads a figure-four grip behind the opponent's tricep to isolate the shoulder. As the figure-four locks, the guard transforms from a pure hook-and-sweep platform into a joint-control hub where the trapped shoulder dictates the opponent's every reaction.

The entry works best when the opponent reaches in to control your collar, posts a hand on the mat to base, or drives forward to flatten your butterfly guard, because each of those actions feeds the arm you need into overhook range. By the time the shoulder lock is set, the opponent faces the Williams dilemma: defending the joint opens omoplatas and sweeps, while pursuing the pass deepens the submission. This makes the transition far more than a position change; it converts a neutral guard exchange into an immediate offensive threat.

Because Williams Guard relies on a shoulder lock rather than collar-and-sleeve grips, the butterfly entry is especially valuable in no-gi where grip-based guards lose retention. The seated butterfly posture provides the elevation and hip mobility needed to angle off, while the overhook supplies the pre-frame that becomes the figure-four. Practitioners who master this entry gain a reliable on-ramp into one of the most dynamic submission-driven guards in contemporary grappling.
conditions: Butterfly guard established with at least one active hook under the opponent's thigh
You have an overhook or deep arm wrap on the side you intend to shoulder-lock
Opponent is seated, kneeling, or in combat base within close guard range
Opponent's arm is reachable across or in front of their centerline, not pinned tight to their hip

variants_and_adaptations.description: The standard entry: from a deep overhook on the opponent's arm, collapse their elbow toward your chest and thread your free hand to your own wrist to complete the figure-four shoulder lock.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent reaches forward to grip your collar, neck, or chest, feeding their arm into overhook range

variants_and_adaptations.description: When the opponent posts a hand on the mat beside your hip to base against a butterfly sweep, scoop that posted arm with an overhook and lock the shoulder before they re-base.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent bases out to defend a butterfly or elevator sweep, exposing a low, isolated arm

variants_and_adaptations.description: As the opponent drives forward to flatten your butterfly guard, use their momentum to underhook and circle their arm into the figure-four while angling your hips out to the controlled-arm side.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against pressure passers who collapse your butterfly hooks by driving chest-to-chest

position_integration: This transition is the main gateway from the butterfly guard family into the Williams Guard system, bridging hook-based sweeping with shoulder-lock submission control. It sits alongside other butterfly arm-isolation entries such as the Kimura and Omoplata, sharing the same overhook setup but committing to a figure-four shoulder lock instead of a finishing crank. Strategically it lets a butterfly player escalate a neutral exchange into a submission-threat hub, and it integrates downstream with omoplata sweeps, triangles, and back-takes that flow from a defended shoulder lock. For no-gi guard players it provides a grip-independent path to a retention-and-attack platform when collar-and-sleeve options are unavailable.

attacker.name: Butterfly Guard to Williams Guard Attacker
attacker.description: How to enter Williams Guard from Butterfly Guard. Attacker setup, overhook to figure-four shoulder lock steps, counters, and drills for the no-gi shoulder-lock guard.
attacker.overview:
As the attacker, your goal is to convert a neutral butterfly exchange into a shoulder-lock control hub by trapping the opponent's arm in a figure-four before they recognize the threat. You start seated with butterfly hooks and an overhook on one arm. The moment the opponent commits that arm forward to grip, post, or pressure, you collapse their elbow into your chest and thread your free hand to your own wrist, locking the shoulder. Once the figure-four is set, you angle your hips away from their free arm to maximize joint isolation and deny them the underhook that would let them escape.

The entry rewards patience and timing over force. Rushing the figure-four against a posted, strong arm telegraphs the lock and invites a frame escape; instead you let the opponent's own reaching, basing, or driving feed the arm into position. Throughout the entry your hooks and frames stay active so that if the shoulder lock is denied you simply retain butterfly guard rather than being flattened. When the lock lands cleanly you arrive in Williams Guard with the opponent already trapped in the mechanical dilemma that defines the position: defend the joint and open the sweep, or chase the pass and deepen the submission.
key_principles: Use an overhook as the pre-frame that becomes the figure-four shoulder lock, not a separate grip you scramble for
Let the opponent's reaching, basing, or forward pressure feed their arm into overhook range rather than forcing it
Collapse the opponent's elbow toward your chest before threading the figure-four to shorten the lever and prevent posture
Angle your hips away from the opponent's free arm so they cannot establish the underhook that defeats the shoulder lock
Keep at least one butterfly hook or leg frame active so a failed entry retains butterfly guard instead of a pass
Complete the figure-four grip to your own wrist for a self-reinforcing lock that survives the opponent's escape attempts
Treat the shoulder lock as a control mechanism first, reading the opponent's reaction before committing to a finish
setup_requirements: Seated butterfly guard with at least one hook active under the opponent's thigh
An overhook or deep arm wrap secured on the side you intend to shoulder-lock
Opponent's arm reachable in front of or across their centerline, not pinned to their hip
Hip mobility to angle off toward the controlled-arm side as the lock sets
A free hand available to thread the figure-four to your own wrist

execution_steps.description: From seated butterfly guard with your hooks under the opponent's thighs, secure a deep overhook on the arm you intend to attack, wrapping over their tricep and pinning their upper arm against your ribcage. Keep your back relatively upright and your head off the centerline so you are not exposed to a guillotine while you set the trap.

Invite the opponent to commit the arm: let them reach for your collar or neck, post on the mat to defend a sweep, or drive forward to pressure. Each action loads their arm into your overhook. Stay patient and keep your hooks heavy so any sweep threat you carry keeps them reacting with that arm rather than retracting it.

Pull the overhooked arm tight and drive their elbow down and across toward your own chest, shortening the lever and breaking their ability to posture up on that side. This bend is what isolates the shoulder; a straight arm cannot be shoulder-locked cleanly, so prioritize folding the elbow before you reach for the figure-four.

Pass your free hand under or behind the opponent's collapsed arm and grip your own opposite wrist, completing a figure-four around their upper arm and shoulder. The grip should sit high near the shoulder joint, not down at the wrist, so the lock controls the shoulder rotation rather than just the forearm.

Shrimp and rotate your hips away from the opponent's free arm, turning your controlled-arm side toward them. This angle deepens the shoulder isolation, takes away the opponent's space to drive an underhook, and aligns your legs to threaten sweeps and the omoplata. Maintain a hook or leg frame on the far side to control distance.

Confirm the shoulder-lock pressure is live by elevating the opponent's elbow slightly and feeling their shoulder bind, then consolidate the position by stabilizing your hips, frames, and figure-four. You are now in Williams Guard Bottom, ready to read the opponent's defensive reaction and flow into the shoulder-lock finish, omoplata, triangle, or sweep.

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens and rips the arm out before you complete the figure-four
common_counters.your_response: Do not chase the arm. Re-pommel for the overhook or switch to an underhook on the same side and reset your butterfly hooks, retaining guard rather than over-extending into a pass.

common_counters.counter: Opponent digs a deep underhook with their free arm to kill the shoulder isolation
common_counters.your_response: Angle your hips harder away from the free arm and elevate with your hooks to break their chest connection, or abandon the lock and hit a butterfly or elevator sweep using the elevation you have created.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives chest-to-chest and flattens your butterfly hooks before the lock sets
common_counters.your_response: Use their forward pressure as momentum: underhook the driving arm and circle it into the figure-four while shooting your hips out, or hip-escape and re-establish frames to recover butterfly guard.

common_counters.counter: Opponent posts hard and stands to back away from your seated guard
common_counters.your_response: Follow with your hooks and overhook to maintain arm connection; if they fully disengage, you keep guard. If they leave the arm behind as they rise, the shoulder lock often deepens, converting their retreat into your finish.

common_errors.error: Reaching for the figure-four while the opponent's arm is still straight
common_errors.consequence: A straight arm slides out of the shoulder lock easily, so the opponent extracts the limb and you lose both the overhook and your offensive position
common_errors.correction: Always collapse the elbow toward your chest first to shorten the lever, then thread the figure-four only once the arm is folded and the shoulder is isolated

common_errors.error: Letting your head drift onto the centerline while setting the overhook
common_errors.consequence: Your exposed neck invites a guillotine or front headlock counter that flips the exchange against you
common_errors.correction: Keep your head off the centerline and to the outside of the controlled arm throughout the entry, protecting the neck while you build the lock

common_errors.error: Killing both butterfly hooks to commit fully to the arm
common_errors.consequence: With no active hooks or frames, a denied shoulder lock leaves you flat and immediately passable
common_errors.correction: Maintain at least one hook or a leg frame the entire time so a failed entry simply retains butterfly guard rather than conceding the pass

common_errors.error: Gripping the figure-four low at the wrist instead of high at the shoulder
common_errors.consequence: A low grip controls only the forearm, so the opponent rotates their shoulder free and the lock never threatens the joint
common_errors.correction: Set the figure-four high around the upper arm near the shoulder so the lock governs shoulder rotation and produces a real submission threat

common_errors.error: Squaring your hips to the opponent rather than angling off
common_errors.consequence: A square position gives the opponent room to dig the free-arm underhook and drive forward, neutralizing the shoulder lock
common_errors.correction: Rotate your hips away from the opponent's free arm to deepen isolation, deny the underhook, and align your legs for sweeps and omoplatas

common_errors.error: Forcing the entry against a strong, defended arm
common_errors.consequence: Muscling the lock telegraphs your intent and burns energy while the opponent frames and escapes or passes
common_errors.correction: Be patient and let the opponent's reaching, posting, or driving feed the arm into range so the figure-four lands on a committed, vulnerable limb

training_progressions.focus: Building the overhook-to-figure-four connection from a static butterfly base
training_progressions.description: With a compliant partner seated in front of you, drill securing the overhook, collapsing the elbow, and threading the figure-four to your own wrist. Focus on grip height near the shoulder and on keeping the head safe. 20-30 repetitions per side per session with no resistance.

training_progressions.focus: Reading the opponent's arm commitment and angling off
training_progressions.description: Partner feeds one of three reactions at 40-50% — reaching to grip, posting to base, or driving forward. Practice converting each into the shoulder lock and immediately angling your hips away from the free arm. 10-15 repetitions of each trigger per session.

training_progressions.focus: Completing the entry while maintaining butterfly guard if it fails
training_progressions.description: Partner resists at 60-70%, actively straightening the arm, digging underhooks, and driving to flatten you. Drill completing the figure-four when possible and cleanly retaining butterfly guard with hooks and frames when the lock is denied. 3-5 minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Hitting the entry against full resistance and chaining attacks
training_progressions.description: Start in butterfly guard with full resistance. Work to enter Williams Guard and, once there, flow into the shoulder-lock finish, omoplata, triangle, or sweep based on the opponent's defense. Reset on a clean pass or a confirmed entry. 5-minute rounds.

flashcards.question: Why must you collapse the opponent's elbow before threading the figure-four?
flashcards.answer: A straight arm slides out of the shoulder lock because there is no bend to bind the joint, so the opponent simply extracts the limb. Collapsing the elbow toward your chest shortens the lever, isolates the shoulder, and creates the folded structure the figure-four needs to control shoulder rotation and pose a genuine submission threat.

flashcards.question: How does the opponent's own action create the entry into Williams Guard from butterfly?
flashcards.answer: The entry relies on the opponent committing their arm forward. When they reach to grip your collar, post a hand on the mat to defend a sweep, or drive forward to pressure your butterfly guard, they feed that arm directly into your overhook range. Letting these reactions deliver the arm is higher percentage than forcing the lock on a defended, retracted limb.

flashcards.question: What should you do if the opponent rips their arm out before you finish the figure-four?
flashcards.answer: Do not chase the escaping arm, as over-extending exposes you to a pass. Instead re-pommel for the overhook or switch to a same-side underhook, reset your butterfly hooks and frames, and retain butterfly guard. The failure outcome should always return you to a safe guard rather than a scramble that concedes top position.

flashcards.question: Why do you angle your hips away from the opponent's free arm once the lock is set?
flashcards.answer: Angling away from the free arm deepens the shoulder isolation, removes the space the opponent needs to dig a defensive underhook, and lines your legs up to threaten sweeps and the omoplata. Staying squared lets them drive forward and underhook, which neutralizes the shoulder lock and stalls your offense.

flashcards.question: Where should the figure-four grip sit and why does grip height matter?
flashcards.answer: The figure-four should sit high around the opponent's upper arm near the shoulder joint, not low at the wrist or forearm. A high grip controls shoulder rotation and produces a real joint threat, while a low grip only traps the forearm and lets the opponent rotate their shoulder free, so the lock never becomes the dilemma that defines Williams Guard.

flashcards.question: How do you keep the entry safe so a failed shoulder lock does not cost you the guard?
flashcards.answer: Maintain at least one active butterfly hook or leg frame throughout the entire entry rather than committing both legs to the arm. With a hook or frame still managing distance, a denied shoulder lock simply leaves you in butterfly guard, so the worst realistic outcome is a reset rather than being flattened and passed.

flashcards.question: What makes this entry especially valuable in no-gi grappling?
flashcards.answer: Williams Guard controls through a shoulder lock rather than collar-and-sleeve grips, so it retains its threat when sweat and a lack of fabric defeat traditional gripping guards. The butterfly entry gives a grip-independent on-ramp into a retention-and-attack platform, making it a reliable way to escalate a neutral no-gi exchange into a submission-driven control hub.

attacker.safety_considerations: The figure-four creates real shoulder-lock pressure, so apply the rotation slowly and stop immediately at your partner's tap, especially during reactive drilling where the opponent may feed the arm faster than expected. Avoid cranking the lock to force the entry; the shoulder is a vulnerable joint and a sudden jerk can injure the rotator cuff or labrum. Keep your own head off the centerline to protect against guillotine counters, and communicate clearly with newer partners before adding resistance.

defender.name: Butterfly Guard to Williams Guard Defender
defender.description: Defend the entry into Williams Guard from Butterfly Guard. Recognition cues, arm-retraction and underhook defenses, and how to pass or stay neutral against the shoulder-lock setup.
defender.overview:
As the defender you are the top or engaging player against a seated butterfly guard, and your job is to keep your arm out of the figure-four before the shoulder lock ever sets. The danger window opens the instant the bottom player secures a deep overhook on one of your arms and starts collapsing your elbow toward their chest. Recognize that pre-frame early: a tight overhook combined with the bottom player angling their hips off is the unmistakable signal that a Williams Guard entry is underway, not a routine butterfly exchange.

Your highest-percentage defense is prevention. Keep your posture, fight the overhook before it deepens, and never feed a straight arm across the bottom player's centerline when you reach to grip or post. If the overhook is already deep, retract the arm along the path of least resistance — straightening and pulling the elbow back toward your own hip before the figure-four closes. When the lock is partially set, a strong free-arm underhook and forward pressure can stall the isolation and let you flatten the butterfly hooks. The worst mistakes are posting a lazy arm that invites the overhook and squaring up into the bottom player's hips, both of which deliver exactly the committed limb the entry needs.
key_principles: Treat a deep overhook plus the bottom player angling off as the primary warning that a shoulder-lock entry is starting
Prevent the entry by keeping good posture and refusing to feed a straight arm across the opponent's centerline
Fight the overhook early, before the elbow is collapsed and the figure-four can be threaded
If the arm is wrapped, retract the elbow straight back toward your own hip rather than circling it into the lock
Use a strong free-arm underhook and forward chest pressure to deny the hip angle the shoulder lock needs
Stay heavy on the butterfly hooks so that defending the arm also progresses toward a guard pass
recognition_cues: The bottom player secures a deep overhook on one of your arms and pins your upper arm tight against their ribcage
You feel your elbow being pulled down and across toward the bottom player's chest, shortening and folding your arm
The bottom player begins shrimping and angling their hips away from your free arm while keeping the wrapped arm trapped
A free hand from the bottom player starts threading behind your upper arm to reach for their own wrist (the figure-four closing)

defensive_options.action: Strip the overhook and re-posture before the elbow is collapsed
defensive_options.when_to_use: Earliest stage — the moment you feel a deep overhook secured but before your elbow has been folded toward their chest
defensive_options.if_successful: You free the arm and return to a neutral butterfly exchange with your posture intact and no shoulder lock threat
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands to strip the grip can momentarily expose you to a butterfly or elevator sweep if you lose your base

defensive_options.action: Straighten and retract the trapped elbow back toward your own hip
defensive_options.when_to_use: Mid-entry — the overhook is deep and your elbow is bending, but the figure-four has not yet locked
defensive_options.if_successful: You extract the arm before the shoulder is isolated and reset to butterfly top with no lock established
defensive_options.risk: A sudden hard yank can feed momentum into an omoplata or armbar if you misjudge the timing

defensive_options.action: Dig a deep free-arm underhook and drive forward to flatten the hooks
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the shoulder lock is partially set but you still have a free arm and forward base available
defensive_options.if_successful: Your underhook and chest pressure kill the hip angle, stall the isolation, and open a path to pass the now-flattened butterfly guard
defensive_options.risk: Driving forward into a fully set lock can deepen the shoulder pressure and accelerate an omoplata or back-take

favorable_outcomes.how: Defeat the entry at its source by fighting the overhook early and retracting your elbow straight back toward your hip before the figure-four closes. Keeping your posture and refusing to feed a straight arm returns the exchange to a neutral butterfly guard with no shoulder lock established.

When the entry is only partially set, dig a deep free-arm underhook and drive forward to flatten the bottom player's hooks. Killing the hip angle stalls the shoulder isolation and lets you advance into a butterfly pass before Williams Guard can consolidate.

common_errors.error: Posting a lazy, extended arm on the mat or onto the opponent to base
common_errors.consequence: The posted arm is exactly the committed limb the entry needs, and the bottom player scoops it straight into the overhook and figure-four
common_errors.correction: Base on a bent, framing arm kept close to your body, or use your free hand for head control rather than posting a long, isolated arm the opponent can trap

common_errors.error: Squaring your hips and chest directly into the bottom player
common_errors.consequence: Squaring up gives the bottom player the ideal angle to isolate the shoulder and chain into omoplata, triangle, and back-take threats
common_errors.correction: Stay slightly offset and angled, denying the bottom player the squared alignment their shoulder lock and transitions rely on

common_errors.error: Circling or yanking the trapped arm across your body to escape
common_errors.consequence: Circling the elbow feeds the rotation the figure-four wants and can hand the opponent an omoplata or armbar instead of an escape
common_errors.correction: Retract the elbow straight back along the shortest line toward your own hip, working with the joint's structure rather than rotating into the lock

flashcards.question: What is the clearest early sign that a butterfly opponent is entering Williams Guard rather than just sweeping?
flashcards.answer: The defining cue is a deep overhook on one of your arms combined with the bottom player angling their hips away from your free arm. A routine butterfly exchange focuses on hooks and elevation, but a tight overhook that folds your elbow toward their chest while they shrimp off-angle signals a shoulder-lock entry, giving you a narrow window to strip the grip before the figure-four closes.

flashcards.question: Why should you retract a trapped arm straight back toward your hip instead of circling it out?
flashcards.answer: The figure-four shoulder lock wants rotational movement, so circling or yanking the elbow across your body feeds exactly the motion that tightens the lock and can hand the opponent an omoplata or armbar. Pulling the elbow straight back along the shortest line toward your own hip works with the joint's structure and extracts the arm before the shoulder is isolated.

flashcards.question: How can defending the shoulder-lock entry simultaneously set up a guard pass?
flashcards.answer: When the lock is only partially set, digging a deep free-arm underhook and driving your chest forward kills the hip angle the shoulder lock depends on. That same pressure flattens the bottom player's butterfly hooks, so a single committed defensive action both stalls the isolation and opens a path to pass into top position, turning defense into offense.

training_progressions.focus: Spotting the overhook-and-angle cue and refusing to feed the arm
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly sets the overhook and begins the entry while you practice identifying the cue, keeping your posture, and avoiding posting a straight arm. Drill stripping the overhook before the elbow collapses. 15-20 repetitions per side at low speed.

training_progressions.focus: Extracting the elbow straight back before the figure-four closes
training_progressions.description: Partner reaches the mid-entry stage at 40-50% while you practice straightening and retracting the trapped elbow toward your hip on the correct line. Emphasize timing the extraction before rotation and avoiding the circle-out error. 10-15 repetitions per session.

training_progressions.focus: Stalling a partial lock and converting to a pass under resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner secures a partial shoulder lock at 60-70% while you practice digging the free-arm underhook, driving forward to flatten the hooks, and advancing toward a butterfly pass. Reset if the lock fully sets or you pass. 3-5 minute rounds.
